title: Top 5 Areas to Buy a Villa in Fethiye
excerpt: Twenty minutes of driving separates a year-round working town from a resort that closes in October. Here are the five areas we recommend most often — and who each one actually suits.

image.alt: Luxury villa with a private pool overlooking the Ölüdeniz lagoon near Fethiye, Turkey

seo.title: Top 5 Areas to Buy a Villa in Fethiye (2026 Guide)
seo.description: An honest comparison of the five best areas to buy a villa in Fethiye — Ölüdeniz, Hisarönü, Çalış, Taşyaka and Üzümlü — covering rental demand, winter life, resale and price per square metre.
keywords: best areas to buy villa Fethiye

body.text: Almost every buyer who contacts us starts with the same question, phrased slightly differently: which part of Fethiye should we be looking in? It is the right question to ask first, because the area decides far more than the house does. A villa can be renovated. A location that empties out every October cannot.

What follows is the version of this list we give people on the phone, including the drawbacks. We have deliberately not ranked them one to five in order of quality, because the best area genuinely depends on how you plan to use the property.

body.title: Before you read on
body.text: Ask yourself three questions: will you be here in January, does rental income matter, and how much does resale value matter? Your answers eliminate at least three of the five options below.
1. Ölüdeniz — the postcard, and the rental income

Ölüdeniz is the image that sells Turkey: the Blue Lagoon, paragliders coming off Babadağ all afternoon, and a beach that appears in every brochure printed about this coast. That recognition is not just marketing — it translates directly into the strongest short-let demand in the Fethiye region, reliably from May through to October.

If rental income is part of your plan, this is the most defensible choice on the list. Lagoon-view villas rent at a premium, and the season is long enough that a well-managed property can cover its running costs and more.

items: Best for: rental yield, holiday use, buyers who want the view they came for.
The drawback: it is a resort. A significant share of restaurants and shops close between November and March.
Watch for: properties sold on a view that is partially built out. Visit in person and check what is on the plot below.

body.text: 2. Hisarönü — the value play

Hisarönü sits just up the hill from Ölüdeniz and offers the same beach access for noticeably less money per square metre. It is the most compact and most walkable of the resort centres, which is exactly why it fills so well in summer — guests can leave the car and still reach everything.

It is also the area most often misrepresented online. Hisarönü is lively, and in July the main strip is genuinely loud. Buyers looking for a quiet retirement base are usually happier elsewhere; buyers looking for occupancy figures are usually happier here.

items: Best for: yield-focused investors and buyers who want the lowest entry price near Ölüdeniz.
The drawback: nightlife noise in peak season, and a very quiet winter.
Watch for: complexes with high shared maintenance charges — always ask for two years of accounts.

body.text: 3. Çalış — flat, walkable and open all year

Çalış Beach is the choice we recommend most often to buyers who intend to spend real time here rather than two weeks a year. The promenade is long and completely flat, which matters more than people expect when they are planning for their seventies rather than their fifties. The sunsets are the best on this stretch of coast, and enough of the town stays open through winter to make January bearable.

items: Best for: retirees, long-stay owners and anyone planning to live here through the winter.
The drawback: the beach is pebble rather than sand, and it is a fifteen-minute drive to Fethiye centre.
Watch for: proximity to the water table — check for damp history in ground-floor properties.

body.text: 4. Taşyaka — town convenience with the bay view

Taşyaka is the residential shoulder of Fethiye town, where the hillside turns to face the bay. It is the only area on this list where you can hold a genuine panoramic sea view and still walk to a working marina, a Tuesday market and a hospital. That combination is rare, and it is why Taşyaka holds its value more defensively than the resort belt.
Supply is the constraint. Elevated plots in Taşyaka are largely built out, so the properties that do come up tend to move quickly and rarely need discounting.

items: Best for: year-round living, resale confidence, buyers who want a view without isolation.
The drawback: the highest price per square metre on this list, and very limited availability.
Watch for: access roads. Some hillside plots have steep approaches that are unpleasant in wet weather.

body.text: 5. Üzümlü — space, altitude and the lowest price per square metre

Üzümlü is Fethiye's highland village, sitting inland and noticeably higher than the coast. Summers are cooler, plots are larger, and your money buys substantially more house. For buyers who want a garden, a view of the mountains and a genuinely Turkish village around them, nothing else on this list competes.

Be honest with yourself about the trade-off, though. You will need a car for everything, and short-let demand is a fraction of what it is on the coast. Üzümlü is a wonderful place to own and a difficult place to fill in August.

items: Best for: buyers prioritising space, privacy and value over rental income.
The drawback: a car is essential, and rental demand is weak.
Watch for: agricultural land designations that restrict what you can build or extend.

body.text: So which one?

If you want income, look at Ölüdeniz and Hisarönü. If you want to live here through the winter, look at Çalış and Taşyaka. If you want space and a garden and you are relaxed about rental, look at Üzümlü. Most buyers arrive convinced of one answer and leave the viewing trip with another — which is precisely why we build the itinerary across at least three areas.
The most expensive mistake we see is not overpaying for a villa. It is buying a beautiful house in an area that turns out to be wrong for how the family actually lives.

title: How to Get a Title Deed (TAPU) in Turkey
excerpt: The TAPU is the only document that proves you own property in Turkey — not the contract, not the receipt. Here is exactly how it is issued, what has to happen first, and where purchases stall.

image.alt: Aerial view over Fethiye bay, where property title deeds are registered at the local Land Registry office

seo.title: How to Get a Title Deed (TAPU) in Turkey: Full 2026 Guide
seo.description: A step-by-step guide to obtaining a Turkish title deed (TAPU) as a foreign buyer: the SPK valuation report, DASK insurance, the DAB currency certificate, transfer tax and what happens at the Land Registry.
keywords: how to get title deed Turkey

body.text: In Turkey, ownership is not established by a contract, a receipt or a solicitor's letter. It is established by one document: the TAPU, issued by the Land Registry and Cadastre Directorate. Until your name is printed on that deed and the registry record is updated, you do not own the property — regardless of what you have signed or paid.

This surprises buyers used to a longer conveyancing process of searches, surveys and chains. The Turkish system is in many ways faster and cleaner. What catches people out is the sequence: several things must exist before a deed can move, and discovering one of them late is what turns a four-week purchase into a twelve-week one.
What a TAPU actually is

The TAPU is a single-page official document showing the registered owner, the property's location by parcel and block number, its share allocation, and any annotations against it. Those annotations matter enormously: a mortgage, a lien, an unpaid tax charge or a court order all appear here, and all of them will stop a transfer.

body.title: Individual deed vs shared deed
body.text: Ask whether the property has an individual title (kat mülkiyeti) or a shared construction servitude (kat irtifakı). An individual deed means the building is legally complete and registered. A shared deed means it is not — and that is a materially different purchase.
What must exist before the deed can transfer
For a foreign buyer, four things need to be in place. None of them are optional, and three of them take days rather than hours.

items: A Turkish tax number. Free, issued quickly, and needed for almost everything else including the bank account.
An SPK valuation report. A government-licensed independent valuer inspects the property and files a report directly with the registry. This is compulsory on every sale to a foreign buyer.
Active DASK earthquake insurance. Compulsory by law, and the policy must be live before the appointment — not backdated afterwards.
A DAB currency certificate. Foreign buyers must convert the purchase amount into Turkish lira through a bank in Türkiye, which issues the Döviz Alım Belgesi in your name.

body.text: The valuation report is the one that most often surprises people, and it is genuinely in your favour. If the licensed valuer assesses the property below the agreed price, you find out before you complete rather than three years later when you try to sell.
The Land Registry appointment

The transfer itself is a short, formal meeting. Buyer and seller — or their representatives under power of attorney — attend the Tapu Müdürlüğü together with a sworn translator, which is a legal requirement rather than a courtesy. Nothing is signed in a language you do not read.

The 4% property transfer tax is paid before the appointment. By statute it is shared equally between buyer and seller; in practice on this coast the split is negotiated, and it is worth agreeing in writing at the reservation stage rather than on the day.

Once the officer confirms the documents and the parties sign, the deed is issued and the registry record updates immediately. You leave the building as the registered freehold owner, with the TAPU in your own name.
The military zone clearance

Foreign buyers cannot purchase inside restricted military zones, so the registry runs a standard clearance check. In practice this is a formality across Fethiye, Ölüdeniz, Hisarönü, Ovacık, Çalış, Üzümlü and Göcek — none of which sit in restricted areas — but the check still has to be completed and it does add a few days to the timeline.
Where purchases actually stall

items: A missing habitation certificate (iskân), meaning the building was never signed off against its approved plans.
An outstanding mortgage or lien annotated on the seller's deed that nobody checked before the offer.
Unpaid property tax or complex maintenance dues, which must be cleared and evidenced.
A DAB certificate left to the final week, which is entirely avoidable with two days of planning.
A valuation report that lands below the agreed price, requiring renegotiation.

body.text: Every item on that list is discoverable before you pay a reservation deposit. That is the entire argument for instructing an independent solicitor — one you appoint, not one the seller recommends — and for running the title search at the start rather than the end.
Do I need to be in Turkey?

No. You can complete under a power of attorney granted to your solicitor, signed either at a Turkish notary while you are here on a viewing trip or at a Turkish consulate or embassy in your own country. Most of our buyers choose to attend in person because it is a genuinely good day, but it is not a requirement and it does not change the outcome.
Ownership in Turkey is a registry entry, not a paper trail. Everything before the appointment exists to make sure that entry is clean.
